t: E-Safety: Smart, Safe and Secure Online
l: Hello and welcome to Mr Butler's Digital Technology podcast. I'm Aoife.
And I'm Conor. This is the Year 10 episode on E-Safety: Smart, Safe and Secure Online.
Back in Year 8 you learned the basics. Keep personal information private, think before you post, and tell a trusted adult if something worries you.
This time we're going further. Your digital footprint, your data, fake news, AI deepfakes, scams, account security, games, wellbeing, sharing images, and the law.
It's a big one, so let's get going. Page one: your digital footprint.
Your digital footprint is the trail you leave online. And there are two kinds.
An active digital footprint is what you choose to share. Posts, comments, likes, photos, reviews.
A passive digital footprint is data collected about you, often without you noticing. Your search history, your location, cookies, which videos you watch to the end.
So even if you never post anything, you still have a footprint.
Then there's your online reputation. That's what people think of you from what they can find online. And that includes what other people post about you, like photos you're tagged in.
Who might look you up? Employers, for a Saturday job or work experience. Universities, especially for courses like teaching or nursing. Sports clubs and scholarship schemes.
And remember, deleting a post doesn't mean it's gone. Someone might have taken a screenshot.
So, search your own name, turn on tag approval, delete old accounts, and post things you're proud of. A coding project, your sport, volunteering.
Good test: would you be happy for it to be read out at your job interview?
Page two: privacy and data. Most apps are free. So how do they make money?
Mostly from your data. They build a profile of your interests and sell targeted advertising. Watch three football videos and suddenly every advert is for boots.
A cookie is a small text file a website stores on your device to remember things about you. Some are useful, like keeping you logged in.

But third-party cookies are set by advertisers, to track you across lots of different websites. That's why cookie banners exist. UK law says sites must ask before storing non-essential cookies, so you can choose reject all.
Then there are app permissions. Camera, microphone, contacts, location. The big question: does this app actually need it?
A torch app does not need your contacts. Choose location only while using the app, and approximate rather than precise if you can.
And watch out for metadata. That's data about data. A photo can hide the date, the time, and even the GPS location where it was taken.
Under UK GDPR you've got rights. From thirteen you can usually agree to an app using your data yourself. And a subject access request lets you ask a company for a copy of the data it holds about you.
Pause and test yourself. What's the difference between a first-party login cookie and a third-party cookie?
The login cookie just keeps you signed in to that site. A third-party cookie is set by an advertiser to follow you around the web.
Page three: fake news, and critically analysing what you see on social media.
Three words to know. Misinformation is false information shared by someone who thinks it's true. Disinformation is false information shared deliberately, to deceive.
Easy way to remember: dis-information is dis-honest on purpose. Mis-information is a mis-take.
And malinformation is true information shared to cause harm, like posting someone's address.
False stories spread fast because they're shocking, and algorithms push posts that get lots of reactions, whether they're true or not.
So how do professional fact-checkers do it? Lateral reading. Instead of reading down the page, they leave it, open new tabs, and see what other trusted sources say about it.
And there's a handy method called SIFT. Stop. Investigate the source. Find better coverage. Trace the claim back to the original.
For photos, try a reverse image search. It often shows a breaking news photo is actually years old.
And a blue tick doesn't prove anything. On some platforms you can just pay for one.
Page four: AI, deepfakes and edited images. Generative AI creates new content. Text, images, audio and video.
And it can now be realistic, and hard to tell apart from real, human-made content. That's brilliant for creativity, and worrying for trust.
A deepfake is AI-made video, image or audio of a real person doing or saying something they never did.
And voice cloning copies someone's voice from a short recording. Imagine your gran getting a voice note that sounds exactly like you, asking for money.
That's why some families have a secret safe word. And the rule is: hang up and ring the person back on the number you already have.
AI can be used for good, like labelled illustrations or special effects. Or to mislead and influence people, like fake celebrity adverts or fake videos of politicians.
You can look for clues. Odd hands, jumbled text, lips out of time. But they're getting harder to spot, so check the source instead.
And one really important point. Making or sharing a sexual image of anyone under eighteen is illegal, even if it's fake or made with AI.
Page five: scams aimed at teenagers. Fake giveaways, free game currency generators, fake shops selling cheap trainers, and dodgy concert tickets.
The red flags: too good to be true, you never entered, you have to pay a small fee, and there's a time limit like claim within one hour.
Then there's the account-recovery code trick. A friend's account messages you: I sent my login code to your number by mistake, can you send it to me?
But the friend's account has already been hacked. The criminal is logging into your account, and that code is the key.
So never, ever share a verification code. Not with friends, not with someone saying they're from the app.
And money mules. Someone offers easy cash to let money go through your bank account and send it on.
That's money laundering. It can carry up to fourteen years in prison, and your bank can close your account. Just say no, block and report.
To report scams: forward texts to seven seven two six, which spells spam. Phishing emails go to report at phishing dot gov dot uk.
Pause and test yourself. A stranger offers you one hundred pounds to let them pay money into your account. What's going on?
It's money mule recruitment. Saying yes would make you part of a crime.
Page six: account security, and encryption.
Use a different password for every account. If one website suffers a data breach, criminals try those same details everywhere else.
Three random words make a great password. Kettle, Fermanagh, Rocket. Long, and easy to remember. And use a password manager.
Two-factor authentication means proving who you are in two different ways. Something you know, like a password, plus something you have, like your phone.
A text message code is good. An authenticator app is better. A passkey or security key is best. And save your backup codes in case you lose your phone.
Now, encryption. Encryption scrambles data so only the intended receiver can read it. Anyone who intercepts it just sees nonsense.
HTTPS is the encrypted version of HTTP, the protocol for web pages. You see it as h t t p s at the start of the address, and a padlock.
But careful. The padlock means the connection is encrypted. It doesn't mean the website is honest. Scam sites can have padlocks too.
And end-to-end encryption in messaging apps means only you and the person you're chatting to can read the messages. Not even the company.
If you're hacked: secure your email first, change the password through the official app, log out of other devices, turn on two-factor, and warn your friends.
Page seven: gaming. Loot boxes are paid mystery rewards. You don't know what you'll get.
And virtual currency, like gems or coins, hides the real price. Here's a worked example. Gems cost four ninety-nine for five hundred. A skin costs twelve hundred gems.
Pause and work it out. How much real money do you have to spend?
Twelve hundred divided by five hundred is two point four, but you can't buy part of a pack, so you need three packs. Three times four ninety-nine is fourteen pounds ninety-seven.
And you've got three hundred gems left over, which tempts you to buy even more.
Loot boxes share features with gambling. You pay, and the result is down to chance. In the UK they're not currently classed as gambling by law.
But in twenty twenty-three the games industry agreed that under-eighteens shouldn't buy loot boxes without a parent's permission. So set a budget and use spending controls.
Page eight: wellbeing. Apps use persuasive design to keep you scrolling. Infinite scroll, autoplay, streaks and notifications.
Likes work a bit like a slot machine. You never know what you'll get, so you keep checking.
Warning signs: losing sleep, homework slipping, feeling anxious without your phone. Keep your phone out of the bedroom at night.
Then there's comparison culture. Feeds are a highlight reel. Filters, best angles, best moments. It's not a fair comparison with your everyday life.
If an account makes you feel worse about yourself, unfollow or mute it. You control your feed.
And influencers. In the UK, the Advertising Standards Authority says adverts must be obviously identifiable. So a paid post should say hashtag ad, at the start.
Hashtag collab or hashtag s p on their own aren't clear enough. Always ask: who benefits if I buy this?
Page nine is about sharing images, and it's an important one.
Consent means clear permission, given freely, without pressure. Always ask before you post or forward a picture of someone.
The law says it's illegal to take, make, share or keep a nude or sexual image of anyone under eighteen. Even of yourself. And that law is there to protect young people.
Sextortion is a kind of blackmail. Someone gets, or claims to have, an intimate image, then threatens to share it unless you pay or send more.
Often it's a criminal using a fake profile pretending to be a teenager. If it ever happens: don't pay, stop replying, save the evidence, tell a trusted adult, and report it to CEOP or the police.
And you are not in trouble. You're the victim of a crime, and adults and police will help you.
There's also Report Remove, from Childline and the Internet Watch Foundation. Anyone under eighteen can use it to get a nude image of themselves taken down.
And if someone sends you an image of another young person, don't forward it, don't save it, and tell an adult.
Page ten: the law, and where to get help in Northern Ireland.
The Computer Misuse Act nineteen ninety makes it illegal to get into an account or computer without permission. Even if you saw your friend type their password.
The Malicious Communications Northern Ireland Order nineteen eighty-eight covers sending grossly offensive messages to cause distress.
And the Online Safety Act twenty twenty-three makes platforms protect users, especially children. Ofcom regulates it.
In Northern Ireland the age of criminal responsibility is ten. And it was only a joke is not a defence.
Some things are legal but still unethical. Sharing a friend's embarrassing photo might not be a crime, but without their consent it's not fair.
Where to get help: a trusted adult first. Then Childline on zero eight hundred, one one one one. Free, confidential and open all day and night.
CEOP for an adult asking for images, or sextortion. The PSNI on one oh one, or nine nine nine in an emergency.
And Lifeline, Northern Ireland's crisis helpline, on zero eight oh eight, eight oh eight, eight thousand.
Let's recap. Your footprint is active and passive, and your reputation includes what others post about you.
Apps collect your data for adverts. Control cookies and permissions, and know your rights under UK GDPR.
Critically analyse what you see. Read laterally, use SIFT, and remember AI deepfakes can be hard to tell from the real thing.
Never share a verification code, use unique passwords and two-factor, and remember the padlock means encrypted, not honest.
Convert gems to real money, watch out for persuasive design, and look for hashtag ad.
And if someone threatens to share an image: don't pay, save, tell, report. It's never your fault.
That's E-Safety for Year 10. Now go and try the quizzes at the end of each page.
Stay smart, safe and secure. Thanks for listening, and see you next time.
